data.text/markdown:
Explain one prediction of an EBM

The global explanation of an Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM) says how the model works in general: see titanic.py for how to ask an LLM for it. This notebook is about the local question: why did the model predict this for this passenger? The answer has two parts, and the split is the point of the design:
  1. The facts are computed, not generated. Python reads the scores and the confidence intervals of the EBM and works out three things exactly. No LLM is involved, so they cannot be hallucinated and they are reproducible.
  2. The LLM only puts the facts in words. It gets the global explanation of the model, the facts, and an audience, and writes the explanation.
The three kinds of fact are the explainability queries of Barceló et al., Model Interpretability through the Lens of Computational Complexity:
Query Question it answers Explanation
Minimum change required Fewest inputs to change so that the prediction flips? Counterfactual
Minimum sufficient reason Fewest inputs that settle it, whatever the others are? Sufficient reason
Count completions With only some inputs known, what share of completions get this prediction? Completions
The first two are exact for an EBM without interactions, because the model is a sum of one effect per feature. The third is estimated by sampling. See the documentation page "Local explanations" for the details and the limits. The cells that call the LLM only run when you press their button and need OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the environment that started the notebook (see the README). Everything before them works without a key.

Load the data and train an EBM

The same Titanic model as in titanic.py. Local explanations need every input of the passenger, so the passengers to explain are the ones with no missing value. The EBM itself is trained on all the rows. It has to be a binary classifier without pairwise interactions (interactions=0).

Pick a passenger

Any passenger works. Passenger 0 is a good start; then look for one the model is unsure about, and compare.

data.text/markdown: Passenger pclass = 3, sex = male, age = 35.0, sibsp = 0, parch = 0, fare = 7.125, embarked = S. The EBM gives a survival probability of 0.11.

The facts, without any LLM

compute_local_facts computes the prediction and the three explanations. Its options (a LocalOptions) are:
  • confidence_level: how sure a claim has to be. Every score is moved by that many standard deviations against the claim, so a counterfactual still flips the prediction, and a sufficient reason still holds, when the model's effects sit at the unfavourable edge of their confidence interval. 0 ignores the uncertainty.
  • min_support: the share of the training data a value needs to be offered as an alternative. It keeps freak values (a 500-year-old passenger) out of the counterfactual.
Move the slider and watch the explanations get harder to prove: more changes are needed to flip the prediction, and more inputs are needed to settle it.

Prediction and contributions

The model predicts class 0 with probability 0.89, and a 95% confidence interval of [0.83, 0.93]. The interval comes from adding the variances of the effects of the features, which assumes they are independent. The contributions are in log-odds: a positive score pushes towards class 1 (survived). Largest first:

Counterfactual (minimum change required)

1 change(s) are enough to flip the prediction, and no smaller set of changes does. After them the other class has probability 0.59.

data.text/markdown:
Sufficient reason (minimum sufficient reason)

Once age, sex, fare, pclass are known, the prediction is settled: it cannot change whatever the other inputs are, and no smaller set of inputs does this. The guaranteed margin, in log-odds, is 0.23.

data.text/html:
Completions (count completions)

Reveal the inputs one by one, in the order of how much each guarantees, and count how many of the possible completions of the unknown inputs get the same prediction. The unknown inputs are sampled from the training data (10,000 samples, fixed seed), so these shares are estimates, not guarantees.

data.text/markdown:
Check the guarantees

The first two explanations are claims about every possible input, so they can be tested. Take the sufficient reason, keep the passenger's values for those features, and fill all the other features with the values of randomly chosen other passengers. The prediction must not change, ever. (This uses confidence_level=0 and min_support=0, so that the claim covers every value, even rare ones.)
With sex, age, fare fixed, 500 of 500 random completions kept the prediction (0). It should be all of them.

What the LLM reads

facts_to_texts turns the facts into one JSON text per explanation. This is the audience at work, and it happens before the LLM sees anything:
  • A layperson (the default) knows no numbers. Scores, probabilities, log-odds and intervals are replaced by words (strongly, very likely), so the LLM has no model number to repeat. The prompt also forbids numbers and jargon.
  • A data scientist gets the scores, the probabilities, the confidence interval and the confidence level, and is told to quote them.

data.text/markdown:
Put it in words

explain_instance needs the global explanation of the model, computed once and prepended to every prompt, so the LLM knows what the features mean and which effects are surprising. Get it with describe_ebm (this is the slow step: one chain per feature, then a summary).
